title: The Patel Brothers Effect: America's Largest Indian Grocer Bets on the Suburbs
excerpt: As the chain breaks ground on new suburban megastores, NRI grocery demand is shifting from basic staples to region-specific snacks, festival sweets and Ayurvedic goods.
body:
The samosa counters and steel chapati machines are coming to the suburbs. Patel Brothers, the largest Indian grocery chain in the United States, is in the middle of an aggressive expansion that reads like a map of where the Indian diaspora is settling next — and how its tastes are changing along the way.

## Context & Background

Founded in 1974 by brothers Mafat and Tulsi Patel on Chicago's Devon Avenue, Patel Brothers grew from a single immigrant storefront into a national institution. The chain now operates more than 50 locations across some 20 states, with its East Windsor, New Jersey store often described as the largest and busiest Indian grocery store anywhere outside India. Many locations pair raw ingredients — basmati rice, lentils, curry leaves, freshly ground spices — with in-house bakeries and prepared-food counters turning out samosas, fresh breads and sweets. For NRI populations, these stores long ago became something more than shops; the Devon Avenue block where the first store opened is now Chicago's Little India.

## Current Developments

The latest move is into St. Johns County, Florida, where the company has purchased roughly 4.25 acres at the developing Shops at Racetrack Road to build a 20,000-square-foot store — its second in Northeast Florida. Executives describe it as a "very modern-looking store" anchored by Patel's Fresh Kitchen, a bakery serving breads, samosas and pizzas, with plans to make the site a hub that could eventually house another restaurant, a jewelry store and a beauty store. The company says it has three Florida locations in the works, part of a broader push the family has signaled toward new markets including the West Coast.

The expansion is calibrated to a community that is both growing and diversifying. As the Better India has documented, Patel Brothers built its loyalty partly by making Indian ingredients legible to everyone — labeling items in both Hindi and English so non-Indian shoppers could navigate the aisles too.

## Diaspora Impact

What's striking in 2026 is how NRI demand itself has matured. Where earlier generations of immigrants hunted for basic staples — rice, dal, a handful of spices — today's shoppers want region-specific snacks, festival sweets, Ayurvedic products and niche pantry items once impossible to find outside India. The shift has fueled a surge in searches for Indian products online and pushed grocers to compete on authenticity, freshness and speed rather than mere availability.

For diaspora families, a new Patel Brothers within driving distance is a meaningful quality-of-life upgrade: fewer two-hour pilgrimages to the nearest big-city Indian quarter, and reliable access to the specific theplas, pickles and produce that make a kitchen feel like home. It also signals that their corner of suburban America has reached a demographic tipping point worth a national retailer's investment.

## What's Next

Patel Brothers is not expanding into a vacuum. A separate boom in online Indian grocery shipping and quick-commerce is racing to serve the same customers, and second-generation Indians — along with a growing base of non-Indian shoppers exploring the cuisine — are widening the market beyond the diaspora itself. The chain's own founders once set a goal of a hundred stores; with new builds breaking ground from Florida outward and an omnichannel strategy taking shape, that number is starting to look less like a dream than a forecast. For the diaspora, the spread of the aisles is its own kind of belonging.
